TI Test retrofitting with competence-based knowledge space theory:
   empirical applications with two educational tools
SO EDUCATIONAL ASSESSMENT EVALUATION AND ACCOUNTABILITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Competence-based knowledge space theory; Retrofitting; Educational
   assessment; Skill assessment; Formative assessment
ID DIAGNOSTIC CLASSIFICATION MODELS; GAIN-LOSS MODEL; Q-MATRIX
AB A critical issue within the educational system is the availability of assessment tools capable of accurately describing the skills mastered by a student and those that are not. Competence-based Knowledge Space Theory (CbKST) is a mathematical theory for the formative assessment of skills that aims to precisely identify the set of skills an individual possesses based on the responses to test items. The current landscape in educational measurement includes lots of good tests designed under theories other than CbKST, which, after appropriate analysis, could be used for skill assessment. Identifying the skills underlying the responses to the items of these tests could enable educational stakeholders to obtain precise feedback about students' mastery of each skill. This work describes retrofitting of existing tests in the framework of CbKST. In particular, it provides a step-by-step guide useful to identify the skills measured by the test and the way they are associated with the items. Retrofitting is illustrated in practice through applications on empirical data collected using two educational tests. Finally, the information about the test, its items, and students' skills that can be gained from retrofitting is explored and discussed.

TI The Road to Quality of Life: Transportation and Outcomes of People with
   Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities
SO JOURNAL OF DEVELOPMENTAL AND PHYSICAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Transportation; People with intellectual and developmental disabilities;
   Quality of life; Outcomes
ID SUPPORTS; ADULTS
AB People with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) face significant barriers when it comes to transportation. Yet, transportation plays an important role in quality of life. Understanding the impact of transportation on people's lives, especially underserved populations like people with IDD, is an under-researched and much needed area; doing so is necessary both to improve transportation and to promote quality of life. The aim of this study was to examine the impact of transportation on the quality of life of people with IDD. We analyzed secondary Personal Outcome Measures data from 2,928 people with IDD (January 1, 2020 and December 31, 2024). We found people with IDD who received transportation had a better quality of life overall and were more likely to have the following outcomes present: safe; free from abuse and neglect; best possible health; rights; treated fairly; respected; use environments; interact with community members; natural support networks; control over personal information; choose personal goals; and realize goals. We need to address transportation barriers to ensure people with IDD can go where they want, both via transportation and in their lives more broadly.

TI In-service secondary school teachers' development of design thinking: an
   analysis based on cultural-historical activity theory
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATION FOR TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE Continuous professional development; in-service teachers; design
   thinking; cultural-historical activity theory
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT
AB Despite repeated calls for developing in-service teachers' design thinking through continuous professional development (CPD), there are limited empirical investigations on in-service teachers' learning of design thinking. Therefore, it remains unclear how in-service teachers, who have established their teaching practices largely aligned with their school cultures, develop design thinking as a new pedagogical framework through CPD. This study investigated in-service secondary school teachers' development of design thinking based on cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) in two secondary schools in Hong Kong. Data were collected from 25 teachers' reflections at four stages during the CPD and two focus group interviews with teachers and training coaches, respectively. While confirming the challenges associated with design thinking CPD for in-service teachers reported in the literature, we provided new insights on teachers' inner struggle with their established teaching practices and their various strategies to learn design thinking. Yet, their learning is still affected by contradictions between the CPD programme and their routines and those between the programme and the school. Our findings imply that design thinking CPD should be adapted to better align with teachers' aspirations and leverage their existing subject-teaching practices to facilitate a more effective integration with the school curriculum. School leaders' communications about implementing design thinking should also be transparent and upfront.

TI Management Students Making Sense: Scaffolding Grand Challenges Through
   Threshold Concepts and Concept Maps
SO JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE grand challenges; scaffolding; threshold concepts; visual mapping;
   visuo-textual assessment; wicked problems; learning outcomes;
   sensemaking
ID WICKED PROBLEMS; EDUCATION; PEDAGOGY; ARTS; PRINCIPLES; PROSPECTS;
   DILEMMAS
AB In this article, we demonstrate how the iterative use of concept mapping develops business students' competencies to analyze the complexity, uncertainty, and diverse views inherent in wicked problems and grand challenges. Focusing on the interconnectedness between business, government, and social actors, coupled with the iterative use of concept maps (as both a teaching technique and assessment tool) proved to be effective and powerful techniques to scaffold transformative deep learning in an international business course. Each subsequent experiential concept mapping exercise supported layers of sensemaking that resulted in deep learning. These layers included: (1) recalling pre-requisite foundation international business concepts and applying these to contemporary grand challenges, (2) sensemaking analytical interconnections between prior knowledge, and relationships between concepts, actors and institutions underpinning wicked problems, and (3) making connections between personal values, actions and worldviews and wicked problems, and drawing on current learning to conceptualize and construct possible future solutions to grand challenges. Our work reveals between-course and within course sensemaking obstacles that can be effectively overcome through scaffolding. We invite management educators to use visual pedagogies to scaffold deep learning and equip students with the confidence and skills necessary to sensemake complex wicked problems and address the grand challenges of our time.

TI Critical Thinking and Social Work Pedagogy
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING IN SOCIAL WORK
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking; social work pedagogy
AB The Council on Social Work Education (CSWE) states that accredited schools of social work have an obligation to teach their students critical thinking skills. Yet, CSWE doesn't clearly define critical thinking but leaves this to at-large members of the profession to figure out. What I do in this paper is describe a philosophy inspired conception of critical thinking. That conception regards critical thinking as reasoning involved in the construction and evaluation of arguments. I next discuss how this conception influences the way I teach an elective on race and public policy that my school offers. I do all this in the hope that the paper can contribute to a discussion in the profession regarding both what critical thinking involves, as well as how our courses might be designed to facilitate the development of this important skill.

TI Assessing the Impact of an Introductory Medical American Sign Language
   (ASL) Seminar on the ASL Knowledge and Competence of Healthcare Students
SO MEDICAL SCIENCE EDUCATOR
LA English
DT Article
DE American sign language; ASL; Workshop; Deaf; Hard-of-Hearing; healthcare
   student education
ID STRUCTURED CLINICAL EXAMINATION; MENTAL-HEALTH; DEAF; RELIABILITY;
   PREVALENCE; VALIDITY; ACCESS; ADULTS
AB Introduction: There are approximately 50 million people in the US who identify as Deaf or Hard-of-Hearing (HoH), of which 1 million use American Sign Language (ASL) as their primary language. Despite this, many healthcare providers are inexperienced when communicating with Deaf/HoH patients. Methods: We designed and facilitated a workshop to teach introductory medical ASL to healthcare professional students, led by a college Linguistics professor and Deaf/HoH individual. A pre- and post-workshop survey was administered to attendees, which measured their self-reported ASL fluency, confidence in performing ASL gestures, and confidence in initiating healthcare-based interactions with Deaf/HoH patients. Results: Thirteen attendees enrolled in the study, of whom 12 completed both the pre- and post-workshop surveys; 9 were medical students and 4 were physician assistant students. Upon workshop completion, 11/12 reported an improvement in ASL fluency, 10/12 reported an improvement in confidence in properly performing ASL gestures, and 9/12 reported an improvement in confidence in initiating healthcare-based interactions with Deaf/HoH patients. Of those with no prior experience in ASL (10/12 participants), 100% of them reported an improvement in ASL fluency. Discussion: This study is the first to describe the development and implementation of an introductory medical ASL workshop for healthcare students. Our results suggest this style of education has strong potential for raising awareness of the Deaf/HoH patient population and modestly improving self-perceived ASL fluency and confidence of healthcare students. Early education in medical ASL is critical to developing culturally-competent healthcare providers and narrowing the gap in healthcare disparities for Deaf/HoH patients.

TI Unpacking the contextualisation of tasks in elementary school
   mathematics textbooks in Turkey and Flanders: the inscription of
   idealised images of children
SO PEDAGOGY CULTURE AND SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Textbook analysis; pedagogical inscription device; contextualisation of
   tasks; mathematics education; cross-contextual study
ID EDUCATION; CONTEXTS
AB In many countries, textbooks are amongst the most central pedagogical tools for teaching mathematics. In this study, we question textbooks as pedagogical tools and instead argue that textbooks function to cultivate normalised images of the child and society. Applying the notion of a pedagogical inscription device and drawing on second and fifth grade mathematics textbooks from Turkey and Flanders, we show how contextualised tasks in these textbooks inscribe idealised images of children. We discuss these inscriptions in relation to specific perspectives on mathematics that emerged from our analysis (a pragmatic perspective focused on usefulness of school mathematics, and an awareness perspective in relation to children's perceptions of the world mathematically), and the educational contexts of Turkey and Flanders, including policy initiatives based on large-scale assessments such as PISA. The prevalence of textbooks in the teaching of mathematics is often related to matters of content and pedagogy, but our findings suggest that this prevalence should also include the production of future citizens.

TI Letters to My Parents: Exploring the Possibility of the Child as a
   Pedagogical Figure
SO STUDIES IN PHILOSOPHY AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Initiation; Mollenhauer's (re-)presentation; Cavell's conversion; The
   child as pedagogical figure
AB Within the tradition of the Continental educational philosophy, the pedagogical relationship is commonly understood as an intergenerational relationship, aptly captured in Schleiermacher's question What does the older generation intend to do with the new one? (Thoomes Opvoeding als opdracht: over Friedrich Schleiermachers opvoedingsfilosofie, Uitgeverij Kok, 1989). An educator is understood to take up pedagogical responsibility when, in brief, they are initiating the new generation to the existing world, while, importantly, also allowing them to give meaning to it themselves (Arendt Between past and future, Penguin Books, 2006; Vlieghe and Zamojski Towards an Ontology of Teaching:Thing-centred Pedagogy, Affirmation and Love for the World, Springer, 2019). In this paper we shift the focus to the child, the one being raised and educated, and highlight an aspect of this intergenerational relationship which we think is inherent to this relationship, but which is mostly overlooked: that also the child can emerge as a pedagogical figure in this relationship. We try to make sense of this through a reflection on a series of letters written by one of the authors to her parents. Drawing on Stanley Cavell we theorize the child's letters in terms of multiple turnings of the self. The transformations these entail express at once a grappling with the "forms of life held in language and gathered around the objects and persons of [her] world" (Cavell The claim of reason: Wittgenstein, skepticism,morality, and tragedy, Oxford University Press, 1979, p. 178) and the struggle to (re)present and make comprehensible to her educators (parents) her way(s) of life. Paraphrasing Cavell, how the child pictures herself within her culture, set against how that culture pictures her (Cf. Cavell 1979, p. 125) brings out the child as a pedagogical figure.

TI Rethinking the Assessment of Oral Communicative Competence in Higher
   Education: Integrating Closed-Ended and Open-Ended Questionnaires with
   Generative AI Tools
SO TECHNOLOGY KNOWLEDGE AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Oral Communicative Competence; Open-ended questionnaire; Closed-ended
   questionnaire; GenAI Tools; Higher Education
ID SELF-EFFICACY; AGREEMENT
AB The assessment of Oral Communicative Competence (OCC) in university contexts is essential, both for its formative value and its close link to employability. However, its assessment remains infrequent and methodologically challenging. This study explores the self-perceived OCC (SOCC) through two different instruments: a closed-ended questionnaire (Likert-type items) and a set of open-ended questions, both developed around the same theoretical dimensions. A total of 112 university students participated. Open-ended responses (OeR) were analyzed using a GPT-4 model refined using prompt engineering techniques to ensure consistency and subsequently validated by expert raters. To examine the degree of correspondence between the two instruments, random forest models were used to predict the AI-based categorizations of OeR from the scores on the Closed-ended Responses (CeR). The results revealed an overall low accuracy, although three items showed accuracy above 70%, particularly those focused on observable and functional behaviors. These findings suggest that open-ended instruments capture dimensions of competence not typically reflected in closed-ended tools, offering valuable insights for the development of richer, more sensitive, and contextually appropriate assessment strategies in higher education.

TI Teachers on a Mission: Experiencing and Evaluating a
   Sustainability-Themed Virtual Reality Educational Escape Room for
   Language Learning
SO TECHNOLOGY KNOWLEDGE AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE High-immersion virtual reality (VR); Educational escape room; Language
   learning; Intercultural citizenship; Teacher education
AB Educational escape rooms are increasingly recognised as an innovative approach in language education, promoting student-centred learning, high engagement, and problem-solving skills through game-based learning. However, the use of Virtual Reality Educational Escape Rooms (VR-EERs) accessed via headsets in language education-particularly concerning teachers' perceptions of their pedagogical value-remains underexplored. This study examines the experiences of 15 language teachers who participated in a sustainability-themed VR-EER grounded in the Intercultural Citizenship Education framework. Working in triads, the teachers engaged with the VR-EER before completing a survey on their experience, providing a professional evaluation of its potential for language learners. The findings indicate that most teachers valued the VR-EER for its ability to promote spontaneous, real-life communication and enhance student motivation through interactivity. They reported a positive experience, highlighting enjoyment, a strong sense of presence, and feelings of connectivity and cooperation during the activity. Moreover, many teachers regarded the VR-EER as beneficial for supporting both language learning and sustainability education. However, various practical and pedagogical challenges were also observed and thematised. The study concludes with implications for the adaptation of VR-EERs in language learning and integration into teacher training.

TI Physiotherapy Interventions for Children and Young People with
   Neurodevelopmental Disorders in Child and Adolescent Mental Health

SO ADVANCES IN NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS

DT Article
DE Physiotherapy; Neurodevelopmental disorders; Children; Child and
   Adolescent Mental Health Services
ID DEVELOPMENTAL COORDINATION DISORDER; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY;
   PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; MUSCLE STRENGTH; DOWN-SYNDROME; EXERCISE;
   PARTICIPATION; PERFORMANCE; PATTERNS; THERAPY
AB ObjectivesChildren with neurodevelopmental disorders make up a significant proportion of the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) population. Early identification of children at risk for developing mental and physical co-morbidities and appropriate multidisciplinary management, including physiotherapy, is vital to improve health outcomes. TI Hearing Faculty Perceptions of the Application of Universal Design for
   Learning Principles in Higher Education Learning Environments for Deaf
   and Hard of Hearing Students
SO AMERICAN ANNALS OF THE DEAF
LA English
DT Article
DE challenges; deaf; faculty; opinions; university; universal design
ID UDL
AB This study explored hearing faculty members' perceptions and practices regarding implementing universal design for learning (UDL) principles when teaching deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) students in higher education and identified the barriers that hinder their application. A qualitative phenomenological approach was employed. Data were collected through semistructured individual interviews with 10 hearing faculty members at a university in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The findings indicated that most participants agreed that UDL serves as a pedagogical framework designed to customize instructional methods to promote inclusive education for students with diverse abilities and needs. Hearing faculty members reported applying UDL through advance planning, making necessary instructional adaptations, and using visual tools when teaching DHH students. The results, however, also revealed significant barriers to implementing UDL. These included limited awareness of and training in UDL principles, alongside heavy teaching workloads and the demands of university instruction, including preparing presentations, designing activities, grading assessments, and providing feedback, all of which were identified as constraints to effective UDL application. Based on these findings, the study recommends developing training programs for faculty that focus on both the conceptual and practical aspects of UDL to improve instructional practices for DHH students. It also suggested creating institutional guidelines rooted in UDL principles.

TI PD-with/for-AI: Framework and Lessons for Responsible Use of
   AI-Generated Synthetic Personas
SO INTERACTION DESIGN AND ARCHITECTURES
LA English
DT Article
DE Participatory Design; AI; Generative AI; Synthetic Personas;
   Co-Creation; Evaluation; Ethics; Interactive Personas; Bias
AB In this conceptual paper, we synthesize findings from four studies at the intersection of Participatory Design (PD) and generative AI to articulate a coupled path: PD is suited for evaluating AI through lived experience; insights inform AI-supported co-creation (e.g., enacted/synthetic personas); and PD, in turn, designs and validates these tools. AB Experience-Based Co-Design (EBCD) is a participatory approach commonly used to improve healthcare services. However, its application in guiding the design of technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI) systems, remains limited. This study adapts EBCD to support nurse-centered design of AI-enhanced electronic health records (EHRs) for patient handover. Our work contributes a technology design pathway that builds on an established method and centers frontline clinicians as equal partners in shaping AI-integrated healthcare systems.

TI Co-Designing AI-Enhanced E-Participation. Insights from ORBIS
   Participatory Approaches to Democratic Deliberation
SO INTERACTION DESIGN AND ARCHITECTURES
LA English
DT Article
DE AI; E-participation; Co-design; Deliberative Democracy; AI-enhanced
   deliberation
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; GOVERNMENT
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in civic technologies, including e-participation tools and platforms designed to support democratic deliberation. Yet, while a growing "participatory turn" in participation is often enacted as a discrete format or early-stage aspiration rather than as a sustained process embedded across the lifecycle of AI systems. This paper examines how Participatory Design (PD) operates as a sociotechnical mediation mechanism in the development of AI-enhanced eparticipation tools and platforms. The paper contributes a structured account of PD as a longitudinal socio-technical mediation process for developing AI-enhanced civic technologies beyond isolated engagement interventions.

TI Suitability of Responsible AI Assessment Tools for MSMEs
SO INTERACTION DESIGN AND ARCHITECTURES
LA English
DT Article
DE Responsible AI; MSMEs; AI Assessment Tools; EU AI Act
AB Micro, Small and Medium sized enterprises (MSMEs) face considerable challenges in adopting Responsible Artificial Intelligence (RAI), including limited technical capacity, a lack of tailored tools, and insufficient access to training and certification. This study investigates the landscape of RAI assessment tools and evaluates their applicability to MSMEs. Through co-design workshops with Estonian MSMEs and analysis of 18 publicly available RAI assessment tools, the research identifies key gaps in the current assessment tools using the lens of the participating MSMEs, particularly in learning support and consideration of environmental impact. The findings highlight that few tools address the specific needs of MSMEs, including cross-sector cooperation and academic partnerships. This research advances perspectives on co-designing future RAI by demonstrating that the dominant paradigm of RAI governance remains structurally compliance-centric instead of allowing MSMEs to have a say. Limitations include geographic concentration and qualitative scope, suggesting the need for more cross-regional and empirical studies. The study calls for a shift from tool centric compliance models to dynamic, ecosystem-based strategies for sustainable adoption of RAI.

TI AI, Metaverse and co-design for social innovation: an application
   protocol.
SO INTERACTION DESIGN AND ARCHITECTURES
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Metaverse; Co-design; Social Innovation
AB Social innovation is a collaborative process that addresses complex problems through recombining resources, constructing networks, and adopting design tools. In this context, generative and conversational AI supports data analysis, knowledge synthesis and the production of operational toolkits. At the same time, the metaverse enables immersive, inclusive codesign spaces that overcome geographical and temporal barriers. The article analyses the potential of integrating artificial intelligence, the metaverse and co-design practices in social innovation. It discusses empirical experiences conducted in Milano and Palermo, developed in the OSMOSI action research project. It highlights opportunities and critical issues in the use of emerging technologies in urban regeneration and cultural innovation processes. It proposes an application protocol. This replicable protocol integrates digital tools and participatory methodologies, with implications for researchers, policy makers, and local actors.

TI Imagining climate-resilient urban spaces: Integrating AI into community
   consultation in Samarinda
SO INTERACTION DESIGN AND ARCHITECTURES
LA English
DT Article
DE community engagement; generative AI; participatory placemaking;
   Midjourney; inclusivity; climate resilience; urban technology
ID VISUALIZATION TOOLS; PARTICIPATION; MEDIA; GENERATION
AB Community consultations in urban planning often exclude participants due to language barriers, limited feedback, and technical complexity. This study explores how generative artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance inclusivity in participatory design. The study reports an action research case in Samarinda, Indonesia, where the AI tool Midjourney was integrated into three community workshops involving residents, civilsociety groups, students, and government officials. Activities combined analogue exercises with structured prompts-crafting and live image generation. The dataset included sketches, prompt fragments, and 133 AI images analysed thematically. Findings suggest that the protocol enabled broader participation across age groups, expanded the range of expressed ideas, and increased in-session legibility and responsiveness of design discussions. Midjourney contributed by accelerating visual iteration and providing shared boundary objects, while the sequenced activities and facilitation structured the feedback loop and made participant influence visible in evolving artefacts. Participants articulated priorities such as cultural identity, local materials, and flood adaptation. Despite challenges related to facilitation, translation, and potential model bias, the study indicates that generative AI can function as an "imagination engine" and boundary object within inclusive, climate-adaptive urban design processes.

TI Human-AI Collaboration in UX: Rethinking Creativity and Productivity in
   Understanding User Needs
SO INTERACTION DESIGN AND ARCHITECTURES
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial Intelligence; UX Design; Creativity; Productivity; User
   Needs; Co-design
AB This research explores the influence of using Artificial Intelligence tools and resources on User Experience practices aimed at discovering and understanding the needs of digital system users. The focus was on creativity, an essential skill, and productivity, a key factor in the job market. The research question revolved around how these professionals can ensure the presence of creativity in their projects when incorporating Artificial Intelligence tools into their workflow, and how this integration impacts their productivity. The aim was to capture a snapshot of the present moment, characterised by constant innovations, by exploring and analysing current uses of Artificial Intelligence. To address the proposed question, a survey, interviews, and a comparative experiment were conducted. The findings in the study demonstrate that Artificial Intelligence has primarily fulfilled an assistive function. Its implementation can boost productivity in operational tasks, allowing professionals to devote more time to higher-value activities. It can be useful for individuals working under high demand or in environments with low User Experience maturity, when facing tight deadlines, small teams, or creative blocks. Artificial Intelligence can foster creativity for some individuals, while for others, it may reduce immersion and lead to less profound or original insights. There is scepticism about adopting it in activities that require creative cognitive effort, immersion, complex decisionmaking, and empathy.

TI Gameplay as Medium: Investigating the Educational Efficacy of Game
   Design in HCI Education
SO INTERACTION DESIGN AND ARCHITECTURES
LA English
DT Article
DE HCI education; game design education; game-based learning; STEAM
   education; serious and applied games
AB Our first-semester HCI course for CS bachelor students at TU Wien discusses different perspectives on understanding and solving problems in CS. Many students do not see the relevance of these topics in regard to their studies in contrast to the perceived "hard skill" courses such as programming or mathematics. Designing game-based learning methods, we aspire to spawn interest and motivation in our students to engage with these topics that are central to technology design and ideally informed by HCI paradigms. Tapping into our master-level course on gameful design, we tasked students to create games for the first-year HCI course. We conclude that our approach was successful, with the first-year students appreciating the games. TI Mediating an understanding of areas of parallelograms: Exploring
   Middle-School Students' Learning from Virtual or Physical
   Representations
SO INTERACTION DESIGN AND ARCHITECTURES
LA English
DT Article
DE Elementary education; Mathematics; Virtual interaction; Physical
   interaction; Embedded cognition and learning
ID MANIPULATIVES; INSTRUCTION; MATHEMATICS; COMPETENCE; COGNITION
AB The use of digital learning environments has exploded during recent years, transforming learning at its core. At the same time, we know little about how this transformation affects younger students, still about to grasp basic concepts in STEM-subjects. This study explores the difference between interaction with physical or virtual representations when learning about areas of parallelograms. 94 middle-school students participated in the experiment, designed as an ordinary classroom activity. The students interacted with a physical deck of cards and a plastic frame - or with virtual representations of these objects - during two lessons. After that they took a test. The results reveal that even if there were no significant difference between the two conditions when it comes to applying the correct formula for areas of parallelograms, the students in the physical condition better grasped the concepts of height and base than the students in the virtual condition. This knowledge, in turn, correlated positively to the understanding of the area formula for parallelograms. These findings indicate that specific actions and/or interactions, facilitated by a physical material and the use of pen and paper, may be truly beneficial for acquiring knowledge in geometry and spatial reasoning.

TI Dynamics and determinants of the career paths of unlicensed teaching
   personnel in Quebec
SO EDUCATION ET FRANCOPHONIE
LA English
DT Article
ID TEACHERS
AB In a context of teacher shortages, several education systems, including that of Quebec, are hiring individuals who are not legally qualified to teach, and whose professional integration remains poorly documented. Drawing on the trajectory method proposed by Loisy, this study is based on semi-structured interviews with 24 individuals, exploring their reasons for entering the teaching profession, their perception of how they were received and their intention to pursue this career. The results indicate that most had dreamed about teaching for a long time, and that being hired rekindled this aspiration. Others mention their desire to contribute to student success or to meet the needs of the school system. Their reception appears varied: some benefit from meaningful support, while others experience a sense of exclusion. A lack of familiarity with procedures and how the school system operates increases the need for guidance. These experiences have varying influences on their intention to continue teaching. In this sense, exploring support mechanisms, professional trajectories, and organizational practices seems essential for reconciling the management of teacher shortages with requirements for quality and equity in education systems.

TI ENGAGING CONTESTED MINORITIZED COMMEMORATIONS: A MÉTISSAGE INSPIRED
   INQUIRY INTO A VANDALIZED BILINGUAL (FRENCH-ENGLISH) STOP SIGN
SO MCGILL JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB . This article examines a case of what we term a contested minoritized commemoration involving the vandalization of multiple bilingual (French-English) stop signs in the Mission District of Calgary (Alberta). We argue that these bilingual stop signs are minoritized commemorations and the vandalization of the French portion of these signs reflects a form of contestation. Drawing on hermeneutic and m & eacute;tissage methodologies, we weave together autobiographical texts stemming from how we individually related to and made sense of this act of anti-Francophone vandalism. Through interpreting our textual braids in relation to one another, we show how such an approach offers relational possibilities for engaging the educational challenges accompanying contested minoritized commemorations.

   BRUNSWICK EDUCATION

TI Exploring the Impact of the Jigsaw Classroom Activity on Student
   Collaboration, Academic Performance, Attitude, and Anxiety in a
   Graduate-Level Statistics Course
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE jigsaw learning activity; statistical anxiety; cooperative learning
ID LITERACY
AB Among cooperative learning strategies, the Jigsaw classroom activity is particularly adaptable, working well across diverse age groups and academic disciplines. This strategy is especially relevant in graduate-level statistics courses, which are notoriously difficult and intimidating for non-mathematical students. This qualitative case study explored graduate students' experiences with the Jigsaw classroom activity in a statistics course within a psychology program. Through semi-structured focus group interviews and reflection papers, participants reflected on the effectiveness of the approach and the challenges encountered. Reflexive thematic analysis identified key themes related to the students' perceptions and experiences. Pre-and post-survey results indicated a decrease in students' level of statistical anxiety. The scores on multiple-choice quizzes also demonstrated students' good understanding of the material presented. Overall, results indicated that students perceived the Jigsaw learning activity as effective in enhancing certain elements of statistical literacy, such as collaboration, academic performance, critical skills, and attitudes toward statistics, while also reducing statistical anxiety. Additionally, participants reported increased engagement and confidence in tackling statistical problems. However, challenges such as uneven effort distribution and initial confusion about the activity's structure were noted. Suggestions for addressing these challenges included clearer instructions and better time management.

TI Revisiting the 4M Framework: Canadian SoTL in a Post-Pandemic World
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Canadian SoTL; COVID-19 pandemic; post-pandemic; 4M Framework
ID FACULTY
AB The Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) in Canada has significantly transformed since the COVID-19 pandemic. Through the lens of the 4M (micro-meso-macro-mega) Framework, this scholarly personal narrative discusses the factors that impact the advancement of Canadian SoTL post-pandemic from the perspectives of seven scholars of varying rank and position from seven universities across Canada. TI Self-Regulated Learning Skills Contribute to Academic Success and
   Academic Resilience in First-Year Students Enrolled in an Online
   Physiology Course
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE self-regulated learning; online undergraduate education; mixed-method;
   first-year students; human physiology
ID ADJUSTMENT; STRATEGIES; MOTIVATION; PREDICTORS
AB Self-regulated learners can independently plan, carry out, and evaluate their own learning process, and self-regulated learning (SRL) is positively associated with academic success. However, youth, limited post-secondary experience, and online delivery are all factors independently associated with poorer SRL skills. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, online course offerings have flourished, creating unprecedented challenges for first-year undergraduate students. Using a mixed-method approach, this study examined how SRL attitudes and behaviours contributed to the success and/or resilience of students enrolled in an online introductory physiology course. SRL skills were significantly associated with students' final grades. High-achieving students also planned to use more learning strategies that are supported by evidence compared to their lower-achieving peers. Importantly, SRL skills also contributed to student ability to improve throughout the term. "Greatest improvers" adequately identified necessary changes to their study methods and were more likely to do so early in the semester, compared to less resilient students. Conversely, an astounding 60% of low-achieving students who expressed dissatisfaction with their midterm exam grades were unable to identify alternate learning strategies to prepare for the final exam. This suggests that having a more extensive "SRL studying toolbox" allows students to choose task-appropriate study methods and to adjust their learning behaviors when necessary. Promoting academic success for entry-level students in online environments requires more than teaching course content. Rather, it necessitates instructional methods that scaffold SRL to encourage students to adopt effective learning techniques and attitudes.

TI Using Formative Feedback to Teach Pharmacy Students to Write Critical
   Self-reflections
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE self-reflection; critical thinking; formative assessment; formative
   feedback
ID ELECTRONIC PORTFOLIOS; THINKING
AB Critical thinking is an essential skill for practising pharmacists. Critical self-reflections have been said to contribute to critical thinking, and formative feedback has been cited as improving student learning. We conducted a two-year study, using mixed methods research, with two cohorts of 1st to 4th year pharmacy students, 76 students in total, to improve their critical self-reflective skills as part of critical thinking. Our pedagogical approaches, unlike the pedagogy of didactic teaching that is historically associated with health professional education, included the writing of critical self-reflections and the use of formative assessment. Students wrote eight self-reflections over four semesters. We provided formative feedback after each self-reflection, which included individual written comments and whole class formative feedback during an explicit instruction class. However, to strengthen the study design we did not provide any feedback between the first and second reflections. Quantitative analysis using a rating scale for the components of knowledge, self-assessment, and critical thinking indicated that students improved in their self-reflections and in their critical thinking, although there were differences between the two cohorts. Qualitative analysis revealed that many students valued the formative feedback and thought it improved their learning, but not all students agreed. We suggest that these pedagogical approaches can cross disciplines.

TI Exploring Student Motivation for Incorporating APA Citation Guidelines
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE citation guidelines; American Psychological Association (APA); error
   analysis; undergraduate students
ID ACADEMIC LITERACIES; DOCTORAL STUDENTS; COMPETENCE; EXPECTANCY; ACCURACY
AB Despite the widespread use of the American Psychological Association (APA) citations and referencing guidelines in undergraduate courses, students continue to make errors, perceiving the task of incorporating these guidelines as burdensome and tedious. To support students' use of the guidelines, various aids have been developed, such as online citation generators, workshops, and handouts, with mixed results. One avenue to examine the errors students are making with the APA guidelines is to explore their motivation. Utilizing Situated Expectancy-Value Theory as our theoretical framework, we explored student motivation for incorporating the APA guidelines into their work, focusing on the components of expectancy, value, and cost. One hundred and fifty-five undergraduate students completed our online survey and indicated high expectancy and value and midline cost when considering implementing the APA guidelines into their assignments. Yet, when provided with an APA referencing task to complete, perceptions of expectancy and value dropped significantly. Students also identified various reasons for their perceptions of expectancy, value, and cost related to APA referencing, such as their reliance on resources to be correct (expectancy), the professionalism associated with correct use of the APA guidelines (value), and the time and effort required (cost). Our results are discussed in terms of recommendations for future support for students. We also address limitations and avenues for future research.

TI "Planting the seeds": A Transformative Qualitative Study on the Impact
   of the "Principles of Belonging in Public Health" Pilot Workshop for
   Graduate Students in the Health Sciences
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE anti-oppression training; transformative research; qualitative research;
   participatory action; public health; health; population health; health
   equity; graduate education
ID FRAMEWORK; RACISM
AB Anti-oppression refers to principles and practices that challenge existing oppressive structures. Training in anti-oppression is not universally offered in population health graduate programs in Canada, and there are few formal qualitative evaluations on students' perceptions of existing trainings in the literature. Therefore, the objectives of this study were to evaluate the impact as well as students' perceptions of a training on concepts related to identity, power, and privilege within the McGill School of Population and Global Health (SPGH) context. A team of students, faculty, and staff designed and implemented a voluntary workshop on anti-oppressive practices for graduate students enrolled in SPGH programs in 2023. We used a qualitative, participatory action design within a transformative paradigm to evaluate the workshop. Attendees were invited to participate in the study's focus groups or one-on-one interviews. Qualitative data was analyzed through thematic analysis using NVivo 12. Of the 37 workshop attendees, 10 students participated in the study. We conducted four focus groups and one one-on-one interview. Participant perspectives were divided into the themes of relevance, safety and social change, collectivity, impact, and participant-driven development of equity training under the pillars of belonging, care, growth, and sustainability. Students found the training effective at improving interpersonal skills. However, they expected more content about addressing systemic forms of oppression within the population health field. The workshop was implemented effectively and successfully established a safe environment for learning. Additionally, this study provides a framework to design, develop, and evaluate anti-oppression workshops in population health education settings using a garden metaphor and demonstrates how the framework can be implemented. Further research and trainings should consider having anti-oppressive content more relevant to the population health field.

TI Disrupting Students' Views of Research One Chindōgu at a Time: The
   Potential of Arts-based Research Experiences in Undergraduate Research
   Education
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE arts-based research; undergraduate research methods instruction;
   transdisciplinary collaboration; critical reflection
ID TEACHING-RESEARCH METHODS
AB Misconceptions about research and lack of engagement are well-documented barriers in undergraduate research methods classes. Active learning and experiential strategies have helped address these challenges. Arts-based research, which integrates creative practices at different stages of the research process, represents a promising pedagogical approach. This paper provides empirical evidence of its potential in undergraduate research education. In Fall 2022, a group of Communication Studies majors collaborated with engineering peers to design chind & omacr;gu, Japanese "useless artifacts" that reject commodification and functionality. This arts-making experience provided Communication Studies students with data for an arts-based research experience. A thematic analysis of eight critical reflection journals from Communication Studies majors in a capstone seminar in Communication and Media Studies revealed that students perceive arts-based research as new and challenging, often leading to personalized and subjective research outcomes. This study argues that the perceived novelty, challenge, and subjectivity of arts-based research do not just facilitate transformative learning and the development of students' research voices; they also provide the conditions to experience and critically reflect on the limitations of disciplinary knowledge production.

TI Do Nursing Students Who Practice Self-care Activities Experience Fewer
   Feelings of Anxiety and Stress?
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE nursing students; self-care; anxiety; stress; nursing education
AB Nursing schools are known for their combination of demanding academic requirements and often stressful clinical experiences. Nursing instructors at a polytechnic in western Canada noted ongoing concerns with nursing students struggling to manage their anxiety. The goal of this study was to understand if self-care activities introduced during each clinical rotation day would help to reduce feelings of anxiety and stress in second-and third-year nursing students. Nursing instructor participants were given a list of the four self-care activities (gratitude list, deep breathing, journalling, and colouring) to be explained and practiced at the end of each clinical day. At the end of the completed clinical session, the participating nursing students and nursing instructors were given a questionnaire to complete during their final post-conference regarding the effectiveness of the self-care activities. Braun and Clark's framework for thematic analysis was employed to answer the research objective. Statistical descriptive analysis was also completed on the post-activity questionnaires submitted by the nursing student and nursing instructor participants. The data revealed that both second-and third-year students identified colouring and deep breathing as the most effective activities in reducing feelings of stress and anxiety. Nursing instructors also identified colouring as the preferred method of self-care for both groups. This study supports the need to include self-care activities in the clinical environment and highlights the importance of developing these skills early in nursing education.

TI Fostering Student Collaboration in an Online Asynchronous Problem-based
   Learning Webtool
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE hybridized problem-based learning, Community of Inquiry, student
   collaboration, classroom technology; apprentissage par probl &
   egrave;mes hybride, communaut & eacute; d'enqu & ecirc;te, collaboration
   entre & eacute;tudiants et & eacute;tudiantes, technologies en classe
ID IMPACT; BEHAVIORS; PATTERNS
AB The scholarly landscape is shifting towards online knowledge production and consumption. Understanding the effect this digital shift has on teaching in practical and collaboration-based contexts is timely since many online applications and webtools are being developed to promote student engagement in asynchronous online courses across a variety of disciplines. The Virtual Mystery (VM) webtool was created for large in-person courses to provide online asynchronous student collaboration in the form of hybridized problem-based learning case studies to small groups of students. This study examines the impact of course delivery (online vs blended) on these group collaborations and quality of work for the VM webtool. This paper analyzes anonymous student survey data from six iterations of a large first-year archaeology and biological anthropology course with two different modalities (online vs blended). Quantitative data was collected from students through course surveys using a Likert scale. Qualitative data was collected from student survey reflections and analyzed in relation to the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework. While the VM exercises create a learning environment that inherently incentivizes critical thinking creating a strong Cognitive Presence for students in the CoI framework, results indicate key weaknesses to Social and Teaching Presence in online learning environments. In particular, this is related to the loss of group communication and the desire for more interaction with teaching assistants and instructors. This study reveals that in online courses, additional course-mediated mechanisms may be needed to facilitate and maintain collaboration/communication between student group members in informal social interactions in online hybridized problem-based learning projects.

TI Decolonization of Academic Practices in Canadian Universities:
   Non-Indigenous Students as Allies
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Canadian higher education; decolonization; Indigenous knowledge;
   Indigenization of learning
AB Non-Indigenous graduate students can play an important role in decolonizing academic practices, thereby supporting post-secondary institutions' efforts to Indigenize learning in Canada. Preparing non-Indigenous students to unlearn colonizing practices and obtaining their proactive contribution, therefore, remains an urgent task. Against this background, the following interrelated questions have been examined: how do non-Indigenous graduate students understand the meaning and purpose of Indigenization of learning? How do current academic strategies prepare non-Indigenous students to participate in decolonizing practices? An online survey with 10 questions was administered among non-Indigenous graduate students at a research-intensive university in Southwestern Ontario. A total of 42 students participated in the survey. The data were thematically analyzed in three major areas, including a) content, b) teaching method, and c) participation in community-based practices. The findings demonstrated some significant improvements in the non-Indigenous students' knowledge of Indigenous communities, traditions, and histories. However, improvements in the areas of teaching and community relations were minimal. The non-Indigenous students lacked practical exposure to Indigenous knowledge-sharing methods, nor were they seen participating in community-based activities.

TI A Study on Faculty Beliefs and Teaching Practices for Student Wellbeing
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE student wellbeing; instructor beliefs; teaching practices; higher
   education
ID UNIVERSITY-STUDENTS
AB This study, conducted at a North American research-intensive university with two campuses, examined the relationship between faculty beliefs and teaching practices concerning student wellbeing. Drawing on results from a 2023 institutional survey (17.9% response rate), the research questions explored whether faculty believe their teaching practices influence student wellbeing, whether they employ wellbeing-focused practices, and if their beliefs align with their actions. Findings revealed that respondents overwhelmingly believed (92%) that their teaching practices impact student wellbeing. In terms of practices, a majority of faculty reported discussing wellbeing topics (55%) and sharing wellbeing resources (52%) within their class. At the same time, some differences were found in the adoption of wellbeing strategies based on years of teaching experience and course level. In terms of alignment, a statistically significant association was found between faculty beliefs about their impact on student wellbeing and whether they employ wellbeing practices in class. This strong connection between beliefs and practices offers opportunities for addressing student wellbeing at individual, support unit, and institutional levels.

TI The Attitudes of First Year Health Students towards Indigenous People
   and Engaging in Mandatory Indigenous Courses
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous; health; mandatory courses; cultural competence
ID PSYCHOLOGY; EDUCATION
AB The purpose of this research was to explore undergraduate students' attitudes towards Indigenous People, Indigenous health care, and how students feel about having to engage in mandatory Indigenous course content. Studies have demonstrated that taking courses with Indigenous content improves cultural competency, thereby improving the overall health outcomes of Indigenous people (Stansfield & Browne, 2012). The exploration of student attitudes toward mandatory Indigenous content is a novel area of study. Health students were interviewed using a semi-structured interview guide. Data was processed using thematic analysis. Student attitudes towards Indigenous people could inform how students feel about engaging in mandatory Indigenous courses. Results support that students overwhelmingly endorsed the implementation of mandatory Indigenous content. It was also found that although students currently feel comfortable working with Indigenous people, they recognize potential health barriers and agree that culturally competent health care can ease some of the health care issues faced by Indigenous people.

TI Evaluation of a Campus-wide Teaching Assistant Training Program
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE teaching; assistant; training; TA; enseignement; assistant et
   assistante; formation; assistant et assistante d'enseignement
AB Teaching assistants (TAs) play a pivotal role in higher education as they spend a significant amount of time supporting student learning and are often perceived by students as approachable and valuable mentors. In recent years, many large post-secondary institutions have offered centralized teaching assistant training programs, as well as in-depth faculty or department-specific programs. However, despite the acknowledgment of their significance, less is understood regarding the development, delivery, and evaluation of TA training programs, particularly ones that are centralized. This study sought to evaluate a newly developed centralized TA training program to understand the experiences of TAs as well as their perceived needs and recommendations to be able to fulfil their TA duties. This is a mandatory, paid training, and is offered through both in-person and online modules to all first-time teaching assistants across all schools and faculties. A unique component of this program is that the TAs are paid for their training hours. Survey data and semi-structured interviews illuminated the level of utility of each learning module as well as gaps that have been overlooked in the training. Overall, the results provide a good understanding of the TAs' experiences with the training as well as recommendations for refinement of the training.

TI From Anxiety to Engagement: Transforming Social Work Research Education
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE social work education; trauma-informed education; social work research;
   pedagogy
ID STUDENTS; TRAUMA
AB In this study, we explore the transformation of social work students from experiencing research anxiety to active engagement in research conducted within a mandatory course at a leading Canadian university. Traditionally, many social workers have perceived a distinct divide between practical social work and academic research, often viewing research methodologies as intimidating and unrelated to their professional responsibilities. The course was reformatted to help students view research as integral to effective social work and consider themselves as potential researchers. Grounded in critical pedagogy, disability justice, trauma-informed education, and anti-oppressive frameworks, this manuscript draws from detailed reflections on teaching strategies and extensive student feedback to propose ten principles aimed at fostering research-informed competencies among social work undergraduate students. These principles are designed to cultivate curiosity, mastery, and enjoyment in research, making this approach beneficial to social work students and anyone experiencing educational anxiety or resistance. This manuscript underscores the importance of transforming educational strategies to help students develop competencies that enhance their professional abilities and personal confidence in tackling new and challenging learning areas.

TI How Can a Departmental Grade Alignment Policy Impact Teaching and
   Learning? Perspectives from Instructors and Students
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL FOR THE SCHOLARSHIP OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE grading; academic policy; ethics; course coordination; grade inflation
AB We investigated perceptions of a longstanding undergraduate course grade alignment policy in a large psychology department at a large research-oriented university. Reflexive Thematic Analysis of instructor interviews and student focus groups led to developing six themes revealing the policy's perceived impact on teaching and learning practices. Discussion emphasizes three major findings. First, this policy influences how instructors design and deliver courses; implementation differences have consequences for students. Second, instructors and students alike worry about this policy's impact on grades perceived beyond the institution. Third, participants situate this policy in a dynamic and relational ethical landscape, connecting it to systemic barriers to inclusion, fairness, trust, and authenticity. This research illuminates many complex ways a department-level grade alignment policy can impact teaching and learning, including unintended consequences and opportunities for change. Broadly, it showcases academic policies as important contributors to teaching and learning context- elaborating a key principle of good practice in SoTL.

AB Opportunities for students with intellectual disability to access higher education in the United States are now more widely available than ever before. Some institutions have developed dedicated programs that support students with intellectual disability to access courses, prepare for employment, and pursue credentials, and many institutions enroll students with intellectual disability even without a dedicated program. Disability resource offices (DROs) are responsible for ensuring students with disabilities, including those with intellectual disability, have equal access to higher education through necessary accommodations and supports. This study sought to address this knowledge gap through a survey of DRO professionals associated with the Association on Higher Education and Disability, the leading organization for professionals engaged in disability services in higher education. Findings of the survey offer implications for supporting students with intellectual disability in higher education settings.

TI Admissions Practices in Inclusive Postsecondary Education
SO JOURNAL OF POSTSECONDARY EDUCATION AND DISABILITY
LA English
DT Article
DE intellectual disability; inclusive postsecondary education; inclusive
   higher education; admissions; developmental disability
ID INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; PARENT INVOLVEMENT; STUDENTS; TRANSITION;
   BARRIERS
AB This study examines the eligibility requirements and admissions processes of Inclusive Postsecondary Education (IPSE) programs in the United States to explore how these structures influence access to higher education for students with intellectual disability. Drawing on frameworks of Inclusive Postsecondary Education, Disability Studies in Education, and DisCrit, this research examines what admissions criteria are used in a subset of IPSE programs, and how program criteria may reduce or intensify existing barriers to college for students with intellectual disability. Utilizing survey responses from IPSE program directors and analyses of the websites of IPSE programs participating in TPSID Cohorts 2 and 3, the study documents 222 distinct admissions requirements. These findings reveal a range of criteria, including guardianship status, documentation of disability, financial prerequisites, academic thresholds, and behavioral assessments. While some requirements appear routine, others may disproportionately burden students with intellectual disability. Although the study identifies patterns of exclusion, it also highlights variability across programs, suggesting opportunities for reform. Limitations include a relatively small sample size and inconsistent demographic data, which limit conclusions about the impact of admissions practices on student diversity. This research addresses a critical gap in the IPSE literature and provides insights to promote more equitable admissions practices. Recommendations for future research are also included.

TI Assessing and Meeting College Support Needs of Students with Disability:
   A Tiered Approach
SO JOURNAL OF POSTSECONDARY EDUCATION AND DISABILITY
LA English
DT Article
DE inclusive postsecondary education; disability resource center;
   multi-tiered systems of support; decision-making
ID POSTSECONDARY EDUCATION; UNIVERSAL DESIGN; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY;
   TRANSITION; PROGRAM
AB Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) is a widely used model for allocating resources to support students in K-12 settings. However, its tiered structure is also adaptable to higher education settings. In this conceptual practice paper, we outline how core supports (Tier I), supplemental interventions (Tier II), and intensive individualized services (Tier III) align with existing and potential postsecondary resources, characterizing programs that provide access to postsecondary education for students with intellectual and developmental disabilities within the Tier III support framework. Three case studies illustrate how the needs of students with various disabilities can be effectively matched with available resources in a university setting with an Inclusive Postsecondary Education Program. Additionally, a decision-making framework for identifying student needs is presented to illustrate how it can be applied to consider college readiness and provide appropriate support in higher education. Ultimately, we propose intentional integration of MTSS into higher education systems to improve access, retention, and outcomes for students with disabilities, particularly those with intellectual and developmental disabilities.

TI Dance of the Stick: Relationships With Children in Early Childhood
   Settings
SO LEARNING LANDSCAPES

DT Article
AB This study explores the relationships that emerged during outdoor play in an early childhood education setting. TI Honoring Story, Land, and Community: Rethinking Indigenous Literacy
   Education
SO LEARNING LANDSCAPES
LA English
DT Article
AB In a Western schooling context, literacy education is often narrowly framed through reading and writing, privileging text-based practices grounded in Eurocentric assumptions about knowledge, learning, and achievement. For many Indigenous children, such framings do not acknowledge the relational, embodied, and land-connected ways literacy is lived and learned within family, community, and culture. In this literature review, we engage scholarship on Indigenous literacy education to examine how storytelling, land, kinship, community, and creative expression open broader understandings of literacy. Rather than approaching these as separate themes or as culturally responsive additions to Western literacy instruction, we consider them as interdependent literacies that reshape how meaning-making, teaching, and learning can be understood. We argue that rethinking literacy in these ways invites educators, particularly non-Indigenous educators, to move beyond deficit and classroom-bound frameworks toward more relational, culturally grounded, and collaborative literacy practices with Indigenous students, families, and community.

TI Critical Religious Literacy as Equity Literacy: Disrupting Silence in
   Teacher Education
SO LEARNING LANDSCAPES
LA English
DT Article
ID PRESERVICE TEACHERS; ETHICS
AB Religious diversity remains a marginalized aspect of social justice-oriented teacher education, leaving many preservice teachers ill-equipped to navigate the complex religious landscapes of Canadian K-12 classrooms. Drawing on qualitative case study interviews with five Canadian teacher educators, this article examines how teacher educators perceive and navigate critical religious literacy as a form of social justice. Applying Gorski's equity literacy framework, we find that teacher educators experience silencing and self-censorship, are concerned about potential harms for preservice teachers, and consider dialogue as a point of disruption. These findings suggest that teacher educators who create intentional space for cultural safety and critical dialogue around religious diversity are better positioned to prepare preservice teachers for the religious complexity of contemporary Canadian classrooms. This kind of dialogic practice constitutes an underrecognized but essential dimension of equity-oriented teaching.

TI Beyond One-Size-Fits-All: Rethinking Spelling Instruction in Elementary
   Grades
SO LEARNING LANDSCAPES
LA English
DT Article
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; KNOWLEDGE; TEACHERS; LANGUAGE; STUDENTS
AB This study examined K-6 spelling instruction through surveys and interviews with 32 teachers (drawn from a pool of 168 eligible K-6 educators) in a western Pennsylvania district. Findings revealed a lack of formalized programs, overreliance on digital tools, and challenges in differentiating instruction. Effective practices included phonics-based and multisensory methods-both cornerstones of the Science of Reading-yet systemic barriers, such as inconsistent resources and limited professional development, hindered implementation. The study emphasizes the need for targeted training in explicit, systematic instruction to improve student outcomes. Implications include developing standardized assessments and robust professional learning. Future research should examine the long-term impacts of these strategies across diverse educational settings.

TI Collaborative Action Research: Cultivating Communities of Inquiry
   Through School-University Partnerships
SO LEARNING LANDSCAPES
LA English
DT Article
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; TEACHER IDENTITY; PRESERVICE TEACHERS;
   EDUCATION
AB This article shares reflections from a collaborative action research (CAR) partnership between a regional university and a rural school in Canada. This partnership involved two university educators, two inservice teachers, and two preservice teachers, all of whom are positioned as knowers, learners, and change agents within this research. Specifically, we worked to center teachers' knowledge through our inquiry into culturally responsive and relevant literacy practices. TI Building China's Independent Knowledge System: The Foundational and
   Guiding Roles of Original Textbooks in the New Era
SO FRONTIERS OF EDUCATION IN CHINA
LA English
DT Article
DE China's independent knowledge system; original textbooks in the new era;
   foundational role; guiding role; challenges
AB Against the backdrop of accelerating the development of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, this paper examines the importance, functions, and mission of original textbooks in the new era in building China's independent knowledge system, focusing on their foundational and guiding roles. Their foundational role is explored in aspects including underpinning core values, systematically innovating the conceptual system, and building on and renewing the methodological foundation. Their guiding role is analyzed from perspectives such as playing a role in shaping national orientation, advancing academic research, building a Chinese discourse system, and transforming teaching models. Typical original textbooks include the unified textbooks for ideological and political education, Chinese language, and history used in primary and secondary schools (including secondary vocational schools). Other objects of analysis encompass ideological and political education textbooks used in higher education institutions and disciplinary textbooks of the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project. This paper systematically explains how these original textbooks consolidate the foundation of China's independent knowledge system in terms of knowledge, methodology, and value, and how they steer the future trajectories of academic development, cultural innovation, and talent cultivation. Additionally, it examines the challenges confronting the development of original textbooks in the new era.

DT Article
DE educational experimentation; Chinese education; independent knowledge
   system
AB Building ' independent knowledge system in education has become a new mission for contemporary educational scholars. Over the past century, Chinese education, as a result of the eastward spread of Western learning, has promoted educational development. However, it has simultaneously led to intellectual ossification in building ' independent knowledge system, diminished ' international discourse power in education, and diluted confidence in ' own education and culture, thereby falling into a dilemma of academic dependency. TI Construction of China's Indigenous Iconic Concepts in Education: A Case
   Study of Life-Practice Educology
SO FRONTIERS OF EDUCATION IN CHINA
LA English
DT Article
DE Chinese education; indigenous iconic concepts; Life-Practice Educology;
   life-practice; life consciousness
AB Indigenous iconic concepts are the basis of building China's independent knowledge system in education, which is characterized by indigeneity, originality, iconicity, historicity, and systematicity. Life-Practice Educology is an emerging educational school in contemporary China, and it is an attempt to rebuild contemporary education. In the course of its development, it has formed two iconic concepts and their conceptual clusters, namely "life-practice" and "life consciousness," which systematically answer such fundamental questions as "what is education?" "what is the necessity and basis of education?" "what is the internal logic and structure of education, and how can these be uncovered?" Moreover, this school responds to the major theoretical questions, including "what is educology?" "what constitutes the independence, uniqueness, and scientificity of educology, and what are their justifications?" By in-depth analysis of the two major indigenous iconic concepts of "life-practice" and "life consciousness" and the generation process of their concept clusters, we can find the basic path of indigenous iconic concept construction in Chinese education. This path involves endowing old concepts with new connotations in the critical reflection of education theory and practice, constructing new concepts with theoretical thinking in the interactive generation of theory and practice, and following the historical logic and temporal logic of the development and evolution of the disciplinary theory system.

TI On Building China's Independent Knowledge System in Education
SO FRONTIERS OF EDUCATION IN CHINA
LA English
DT Article
DE Chinese education; independent knowledge system; disciplinary system;
   academic system; discourse system
AB The formation of an independent knowledge system marks a mature discipline, prosperous scholarship, and self-conscious discourse of Chinese education. Originating from the eastward spread of Western learning, Chinese education repeatedly suffered from overwhelming destruction for more than a century. However, Chinese education has consistently taken national character and historical continuity as the main thread of independent knowledge construction, contemporaneity and originality as a powerful drive for knowledge development, and systematic nature and specialized nature as a basis of social identity. Chinese education has increasingly highlighted its properties in people's well-being, national strategy, and political arena with changing times for more than 70 years since the founding of the People's Republic of China. China's independent knowledge system in education consists of the disciplinary system, academic system, discourse system, textbook system, and governance system. Specifically, it is composed of iconic concepts, core knowledge, and cutting-edge knowledge in terms of content form. The knowledge production of Chinese education is achieved by academic disciplines, schools, societies, and publications. The knowledge development is propelled by the transformation and application of practice knowledge, policy knowledge, and educational thoughts. The characteristics of Chinese education stem from the traditions, practices, and problems of Chinese education and are based on disciplinary consciousness, academic autonomy, and cultural confidence. It is imperative to properly cope with the dialectics of Chinese characteristics and general knowledge, lay a solid foundation of the education discipline, and ignite originality in the academic system. Additionally, it is necessary to enhance the guiding role of the textbook system and improve the effectiveness of the governance system. These efforts all aim to promote clear articulation, regular adoption, worldwide spreading, and the powerful impact of Chinese education, thereby providing guidance for thoughts and the foundation of theories for building a leading country in education.

TI ETHNOBOTANICAL INTEGRATION IN SCHOOL EDUCATION
SO REVISTA CONRADO
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Ethnobotanical; School Education; Biodiversity; Traditional Medicine
ID MEDICINAL-PLANTS
AB Ethnobotany, when approached through education, allows for the preservation and conservation of biocultural heritage. This research aims to analyze the integration of ethnobotany into school education. To this end, the study was conducted using the PRISMA methodology, with a descriptive and retrospective approach, complemented by a bibliometric analysis and the co-occurrence method, employing the tools of the VosViewer package. The results established six main categories: ethnobotany, education, traditional knowledge, medicinal plants, biodiversity, and traditional medicine. The study demonstrated the relevance of integrating ethnobotany into school education, as ethnobotanical knowledge for teaching science can be an excellent way to engage students, help them learn scientific concepts more meaningfully, and develop a deeper appreciation of their environment and local culture.

AB Teaching physics to students with hearing impairments is important to ensure equitable access to education regardless of students' abilities or disabilities. Furthermore, physics is a necessary discipline that provides the foundation for understanding the world around us and allows for the development of critical thinking and skills essential to society. The objective of this study is to conduct a bibliometric analysis of physics education for students with hearing impairments. TI THE LITERARY CONTINUUM AND PEDAGOGY OF CRITICAL DISCOURSE IN LATIN
   AMERICA: FROM THE OPEN VEINS
SO REVISTA CONRADO
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE critical thinking; Latin American literature; critical pedagogy;
   historical memory; transformative education
AB This study analyzes the Latin American literary continuum as a pedagogical mediator in the development of critical thinking, based on a qualitative interpretative approach grounded in the socio-critical paradigm. Through a documentary-analytical design, supported by hermeneutic-interpretative methods and critical discourse analysis, representative works of Latin American thought are examined, highlighting Open Veins of Latin America by Eduardo Galeano as the central axis. The findings reveal that critical literature integrates historical memory, the visibility of subaltern voices, discursive strategies, and ethical formation, positioning itself as a comprehensive pedagogical resource. Furthermore, literary narratives enable the understanding of domination and resistance dynamics in Latin America, fostering analytical, reflective, and socially engaged competencies. The study concludes that the literary continuum significantly contributes to the reconfiguration of contemporary educational thought by integrating interdisciplinary dimensions and promoting a transformative pedagogy that develops critical and socially committed individuals. In this regard, literature emerges as a strategic tool in educational processes, capable of linking knowledge, historical awareness, and social action.

However, local potentialities were also identified that can be leveraged through educational, training, and inter-institutional coordination strategies. In conclusion, the study proposes strengthening territorial governance and implementing educational and strategic approaches that encourage the active participation of local stakeholders in order to build a socioeconomic development agenda aligned with the needs and expectations of rural youth.

TI Self-Determined Schools: Lumbee Education History in aTri-racial System
   in Robeson County, North Carolina
SO HISTORICAL STUDIES IN EDUCATION-CANADA
LA English
DT Article
AB In 1885, North Carolina recognized the Croatan Indians as a third race in addition to Whites and Blacks, granting them state apportionments and a self-governed public school system in Robeson County. This legislation also established a tri-racial school system in the state. Over time, the Croatans, renamed Lumbee, became the largest tribe in the southeastern US. Despite racialization and ongoing appeals for additional school funding, the Lumbee found strength in their self-determination. They supported their schools through educational rallies and contributions of land, supplies, time, and labour. The Lumbee ancestors were committed to creating and maintaining community schools, a legacy that remains central to Robeson County and North Carolina's history. This article traces the history of Lumbee-controlled schools from 1885 to 1940.
